summary: This informational document registers the application/yaml media type with IANA, along with the +yaml structured syntax suffix. They identify content serialized according to the YAML specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Files get a label that says what they are. This gives YAML files an official label so programs know how to read them.

subtitle: Official IANA registration for the application/yaml media type and +yaml suffix.

tldr.problem: YAML is widely used on the Internet for configuration files and APIs, but it lacked an official IANA media type registration. Applications could not reliably use content negotiation to request or declare YAML content, and non-standard names like application/x-yaml were used instead.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the application/yaml media type with IANA and also defines a +yaml structured syntax suffix. These registrations follow existing standards for media type registration and include security, interoperability, and fragment identifier considerations specific to YAML.
tldr.outcome: YAML content now has an official IANA-registered media type, enabling proper content negotiation on the web and in APIs. HTTP clients and servers can use the Accept and Content-Type headers to work with YAML files correctly.

today: RFC 9512 is an Informational RFC published in February 2024. The application/yaml media type and +yaml suffix are now registered in the IANA registry. Web servers and applications can use these officially registered types in Content-Type and Accept headers. The registry entries enable proper content negotiation for YAML content across the Internet.

sections.title: What Is YAML and Why Register It?
sections.content:
YAML stands for YAML Ain't Markup Language. It is a human-friendly data serialization format that is widely used on the Internet for configuration files, API specifications like OpenAPI, and data interchange. Unlike XML or JSON, YAML emphasizes readability by using indentation and simple syntax that resembles natural language.

YAML has been used informally with unregistered media types like application/x-yaml or text/x-yaml for years. However, to enable proper content negotiation—where an HTTP client can request YAML format and a server can declare the response is YAML—an official IANA-registered media type is necessary. This RFC registers application/yaml as the official media type and defines +yaml as a structured syntax suffix for media types based on YAML.
sections.plainLanguage: Websites use labels like "this is HTML" or "this is JSON" in HTTP headers. YAML didn't have an official label, so programs had to guess. Now it has a real, official label.

sections.title: The Registrations: application/yaml and +yaml
sections.content:
The RFC registers application/yaml as the primary media type for YAML documents. It specifies that YAML files use binary encoding considerations and that both .yaml (preferred) and .yml filename extensions map to this media type. The media type supports optional fragment identifiers to point to specific nodes within a YAML document.

The RFC also defines +yaml as a structured syntax suffix. This allows other media types to indicate they are YAML-based by using a name like application/custom+yaml. For example, an API specification format built on YAML could register as application/openapi+yaml. Like other structured syntax suffixes, +yaml provides common security and interoperability considerations that apply to any media type using it.
sections.plainLanguage: application/yaml is the label for regular YAML files. The +yaml part lets other formats say "I'm built on YAML but with extra stuff."

sections.title: YAML and JSON Compatibility Issues
sections.content:
YAML is a superset of JSON, meaning all JSON documents are valid YAML. However, YAML has features that JSON does not support, which can cause interoperability problems. YAML supports non-string keys in mappings, anchor-based references and aliases (like pointers in other languages), comments, custom data types (tags), and cyclic references.

When YAML must be converted to or used with JSON, these YAML-specific features may be lost or cause errors. For example, an alias node that references another node multiple times will be replaced by static copies of the value when converted to JSON. Multi-document YAML streams (multiple independent documents in one file) have no direct JSON equivalent. Programs that process both YAML and JSON must define which YAML features they accept and how to handle unsupported ones.
sections.plainLanguage: YAML is more flexible than JSON, so YAML files can have things JSON doesn't understand. If you convert them, you might lose information.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
YAML deserialization has security implications that applications must handle carefully. Some YAML implementations allow tags that trigger arbitrary code execution (e.g., !!python/object). This must be disabled by default in any safe YAML parser. Applications should use safe deserializers and avoid processing YAML from untrusted sources unless the input is validated first.

YAML's support for references and aliases can also cause denial-of-service issues if not handled carefully. A malicious YAML document can create cyclic references or exponential expansion (like a billion laughs attack) that causes the parser to consume excessive memory or CPU. YAML processors should limit recursion depth and validate input before processing.

The registration also addresses the evolution of YAML itself. The YAML specification has changed over versions, with some features added and others removed. The media type registration is version-independent, allowing content negotiation to work regardless of YAML version. Applications concerned with specific versions can use the %YAML directive inside their documents to specify the version explicitly.
sections.plainLanguage: YAML parsers need to be careful because some YAML features can be dangerous—like code that runs automatically or tricks that create infinite loops. Safe libraries exist, and programs should use them.
